items.stem: Which line of defence involves the skin and mucous membranes?
items.note: Barrier defences come first: skin, mucous membranes, secretions. Innate (second) and adaptive (third) lines act once pathogens get in.

items.stem: During blood clotting, fibrin is produced from fibrinogen by the action of:
items.note: Clotting cascade: platelets + clotting factors → thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin fibres, forming the clot mesh.

items.stem: Which cells carry out phagocytosis of pathogens as part of the innate immune response?
choices: Phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages
items.note: Neutrophils respond fast and die quickly; macrophages are larger, longer-lived and can present antigens. Both engulf and digest pathogens.

items.stem: Histamine released during an infection causes:
items.note: Vasodilation + leaky capillaries bring more immune cells to the area — causing redness, heat, swelling and pain (inflammation). Antihistamines counteract this.

items.stem: Antibodies are produced by:
items.note: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies; memory cells persist for long-term immunity.

items.stem: The variable region of an antibody:
items.note: The tips of the Y contain the variable regions — unique shape/charge complementarity to ONE antigen. The constant region determines the antibody's class and interactions.

items.stem: How many antigen-binding sites does one antibody molecule have?
items.note: Y-shaped structure with two identical antigen-binding sites (one on each arm) — this allows cross-linking of antigens.

items.stem: Compared with the primary immune response, the secondary response is:
choices: Faster and stronger — due to memory cells
Identical — memory cells do not affect it
items.note: Memory cells trigger rapid production of antibodies on re-exposure: shorter lag, higher peak, longer duration. The classic graph shows two peaks.

items.stem: A vaccine typically contains:
choices: Antigens from the pathogen (attenuated, inactivated or fragments)
items.note: Vaccines present antigens without causing disease — the immune system builds memory cells. Some vaccines are live attenuated, others inactivated, subunit or mRNA.

items.stem: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals because:
choices: The vaccine spreads from person to person
Pathogen transmission is reduced when most of the population is immune
Unvaccinated people develop memory cells by contact
The pathogen mutates to a harmless form
items.note: When enough people are immune, chains of transmission are broken — even susceptible individuals rarely meet the pathogen. Thresholds depend on the disease's R₀.

items.stem: Antibiotics are effective against:
items.note: Antibiotics target bacterial structures/processes (cell wall, ribosomes, DNA gyrase). Viruses lack these targets — which is why colds cannot be treated with antibiotics.

items.stem: Antibiotic resistance arises because:
choices: Bacteria learn to avoid the antibiotic
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing resistance genes on
items.note: Selection pressure: resistant cells survive treatment, reproduce and pass on resistance genes (plasmids). Misuse and incomplete courses accelerate this.

items.stem: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by:
choices: Fusing a B lymphocyte with a myeloma (cancer) cell — a hybridoma
Isolating them from any patient's blood
items.note: Hybridomas divide indefinitely AND secrete one specific antibody — large quantities of identical (monoclonal) antibodies.

items.stem: A pregnancy test detects the hormone hCG using:
choices: Antibodies specific to hCG on a test strip
items.note: Monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG are attached to a coloured marker on the strip — hCG in urine binds and produces the visible line.

items.stem: HIV attacks the immune system by destroying:
items.note: HIV is a retrovirus: reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, which integrates into the host genome. Loss of helper T cells collapses adaptive immunity → AIDS.

items.stem: An allergy involves an immune response to:
items.note: Allergies: the immune system overreacts to harmless antigens (pollen, dust). Mast cells release histamine → allergy symptoms; antihistamines block this.

items.stem: Type 1 diabetes is an example of:
choices: An autoimmune disease — the immune system attacks the body's own cells
items.note: Autoimmunity: immune attack on the body's own cells — in type 1 diabetes the β cells of the pancreas are destroyed. Other examples: rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis.

items.stem: Antibodies in breast milk provide the infant with:
items.note: Passive immunity = receiving antibodies made by another individual. No memory cells are produced, so protection is temporary — but immediate.

items.stem: A fever above the normal body temperature helps against infection because:
choices: It denatures the pathogen's enzymes completely
Higher temperature inhibits pathogen reproduction and increases immune activity
items.note: A moderate fever slows pathogen reproduction and boosts immune cell activity. Very high fevers are dangerous — the control system matters.

items.stem: Vaccination programs aim to create:
choices: Artificial active immunity — memory cells without disease
items.note: Artificial ACTIVE immunity: the body produces its own antibodies + memory cells after antigen exposure (vaccine). Passive = receiving ready-made antibodies.

items.stem: A person is exposed to the same pathogen twice, one year apart. Draw or describe the antibody concentration over time and explain the differences between the two responses.
markscheme: Primary response: slow rise, lower peak, shorter duration — lag while B cells are activated (1)
Memory cells formed during the primary response persist (1)
Secondary response: faster rise, higher peak, longer duration (1)
Reason: memory B cells are already present and divide rapidly into plasma cells (1)
items.tactic: The immune-response graph is a standard data question: label both peaks, mark the lag phase, and tie every feature to memory cells.

items.stem: Explain why antibiotic resistance is increasing, and state one measure that helps slow its spread.
markscheme: Antibiotics create a selection pressure — resistant bacteria survive treatment (1)
Resistant bacteria reproduce and pass resistance genes to other bacteria (1)
Misuse accelerates it: incomplete courses, use for viral infections, overuse in livestock (1)
Measures: complete prescribed courses, only use antibiotics for bacterial infections, hygiene to limit spread (any one) (1)
items.tactic: Selection-pressure answers follow the evolution pattern: variation → selection → reproduction of resistant cells → increased resistance in the population.
